newsitem.title: UK: Urals talked firm but sceptics doubt $1 discount.
newsitem.headline: Urals talked firm but sceptics doubt $1 discount.

text.p: Russian Urals crude was steady in a quiet Mediterranean market on Thursday but traders doubted the crude was as strong as the $1 discount reportedly achieved for two cargoes on Wednesday.

Traders said they had heard values of Dated -$1/$1.05 agreed between trading houses for the million-barrel Biruinta loading June 27-29 and a discount of around $1 for the million barrel Cuban loading June 22-24.

Both private and confidential trades, if confirmed, would represent a big 10 to 15 cent rise from the last traded level, reflecting the scarcity of sours in the Mediterranean and good demand sparked by strong refinery margins.
But traders had their suspicions.
"These numbers are not real. It looks like inter-trade play. Only when I see a refinery paying those levels will I believe it," one trader said.
The buyer of the Cuban reportedly has a short into Greece and was seen trying to move the market higher.
"As for the Biruinta, from a trade perspective it makes no sense, but it does make sense from a (paper) pricing perspective," the trader said.

"Whether they are just inter-trade plays is not clear," another trader commented. "There may have been some traders ready to buy Urals because Kirkuk is late appearing on the market, so they have taken the view that there are very few sours around and have seized the opportunity to buy.
"But -$1.15 sounds like the more real value to me."
An 80,000 tonne cargo of Urals loading 20-22 was moved at a discount of around $1.10 to $1.15 on Tuesday.

Most of the first and second decade Urals programme has been committed, dealers say. Many traders were not expecting first liftings of Iraqi Kirkuk under the second term of the United Nations oil-for-food agreement to start until July.
Asian buying interest has been taking centre stage on the lacklustre West African market, but details, including prices, remained private and confidential.
Traders said China's Unipec and Sinochem have been buying more than 10 cargoes of Palanca, Qua Iboe, Zafiro and Cabinda, mostly for July lifting, while South Korea and Taiwan have also been active.
"The arb is wide open and this is very cheap oil for them," one trader said. "In July I'd expect them to take more than they took in June, and we might expect it to hold its values."
Some six million barrels of Nigerian grades are estimated to remain for June while, traders said, and overall the market looks depressed by large supply.

"This market looks awful," said a trader at a European major. "When you have some more North Sea capacity coming back next month, and with the Iraqis coming back as well, you have to wonder how much further the market will fall."
Bonny Light was assessed two to three cents weaker at Dated +40 cents, Qua at Dated +28 cents and Forcados +12 cents.
Asia imported 500,000 barrels per day (bpd) of West African crude in first half 1997, Ian Taylor, Vitol Group of Companies president told an oil conference in Malaysia on Monday.

He said tighter specifications for oil products and rising refinery capacity were supporting the demand for West African crudes. Taylor's estimate would indicate that imports of West African grades slowed in the second quarter of 1997.
-- William Maclean, London newsroom +44 171 542 7646
